summary:
Our solution integrates the organization and optimization of existing data to predict an elevated risk of developing Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS).

To monitor astronauts’ physiological parameters in real time, we rely on the Canadian Bio-Monitor and Bio-Analyzer systems.

In addition to the existing measurements, we propose assessing the Translaminar Pressure Difference (TLPD) across the Lamina Cribrosa, between Intraocular Pressure (IOP) and Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Pressure within the Optic Nerve Sheath.

Measurements will be performed before and during spaceflight. A change in this pressure difference exceeding a predefined threshold will be considered an indicator of elevated SANS risk.

Furthermore, we propose incorporating Lymphatic Drainage Massage into existing astronaut exercise routines, with the aim of promoting Edema Clearance through the Lymphatic System and supporting healthy Blood Circulation.
details:
HMSA is a personalized in-flight health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions. Space does not affect every body the same way: two astronauts on the same mission can come home with very different health outcomes. HMSA therefore starts from each individual astronaut rather than from a population average. Our first clinical module targets Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), in which the headward fluid shift and intracranial pressure changes of microgravity cause optic disc edema, posterior globe flattening, choroidal folds and a hyperopic shift in vision.

The system works in four stages. First, before launch, it builds a multi-dimensional baseline for each astronaut from clinical, biochemical, genetic and high-resolution anatomical data. Second, during flight, it monitors the physiological, biochemical and structural metrics that matter for that astronaut’s risk profile, periodically or continuously. Third, it applies gradient-based deviation analysis: rather than only asking whether a value is abnormal, it tracks how fast each biomarker is changing and compares that trajectory with normal adaptation to microgravity versus pathological trends derived from historical astronaut data. Fourth, it turns detected anomalies into graded, evidence-based countermeasure recommendations, which the flight surgeon reviews before any treatment begins.

Monitoring is risk-stratified. HMSA weights each astronaut’s genetic and physiological risk factors to set how often they are tested and how strict their alert thresholds are, combining systemic metabolism and organ-specific imaging into one real-time vulnerability index. For SANS, the integrated risk factors are: SANS on a previous mission, the strongest known predictor; one-carbon metabolism genetics, including polymorphisms in MTRR, SHMT1 and MTHFR, with the G allele of MTRR A66G and the C allele of SHMT1 C1420T as risk alleles; vitamin B status, measured directly and through the functional markers homocysteine and methylmalonic acid; and the optic nerve head on 3D OCT, where a smaller optic cup before flight indicates higher risk, and a thickening neuroretinal rim with a shrinking cup during flight signals developing swelling. When these signals converge, for example a shrinking cup together with impaired one-carbon metabolism and rising homocysteine, HMSA automatically escalates to closer surveillance and recommends targeted countermeasures: personalized B-complex and folate support, fluid-redistribution methods such as lymphatic drainage massage, and mechanical aids such as lower body negative pressure.

The benefits are earlier detection, personalized care and autonomy. Because every measurement is compared to the astronaut’s own baseline and trajectory, HMSA can identify risk before damage becomes visible. Because monitoring intensity scales with risk, high-risk astronauts get closer attention without overloading everyone else’s schedule. And because analysis runs on board, it supports deep-space missions where specialists are unavailable and communication with Earth is delayed.

Our intended impact is to protect astronauts’ long-term vision on missions to the Moon and Mars, and to shift spaceflight medicine from diagnosis after the fact to prediction and prevention. SANS is the first module; the same architecture of baseline, monitoring, gradient analysis and countermeasures can be extended to other spaceflight risks such as bone loss, muscle loss and radiation exposure.

We built the frontend as a web application in JavaScript using React, Vite and React Router, with recharts for biomarker trend charts and CSS for styling. Its centerpiece is a hand-built 2D SVG cross-section of the eye and optic nerve, in which more than 50 anatomical structures and all retinal layers in an OCT-style view can glow red (alert), yellow (watch) or green (selected), so astronauts see their status at a glance. All data flows through a single service layer, currently using realistic mock data, so a backend can be connected without changing the interface. We used Claude Code for development, GitHub for version control and Vercel for deployment. On the hardware side, HMSA is designed to use equipment already in orbit: the Canadian Space Agency’s Bio-Monitor and Bio-Analyzer for physiological and lab data, and the OCT and ultrasound imaging already used for SANS research on the International Space Station.

HMSA is creative in its focus on the individual. Instead of one monitoring schedule for every astronaut, it adjusts surveillance to each person’s risk. Instead of fixed thresholds, it analyzes the speed and direction of change. And instead of looking at genetics, blood chemistry and imaging separately, it looks for the moment they converge. The eye avatar turns complex medical data into something an astronaut can understand in seconds.

Our team designed around the astronaut’s real constraints. Crew time is scarce, so after mentor feedback we built a minimalist home screen that answers two questions: “Am I okay?” and “What do I do now?” We used plain language first with medical terms second, large touch targets for use in microgravity, and emergency steps that work without waiting for Earth. We kept the flight surgeon in the loop for every treatment decision and labeled medical content as pending expert review. We also chose transparent, explainable analysis over a black-box model, because public astronaut data is limited and both astronauts and doctors need to see why an alert was raised.
